## Self-questions and worked answers

148 answered questions revisit this report's scope. Each answer retains the same source links as the teaching module; calculations and debugging examples are informative.

### Q01. What is the governing interpretation for “Reading map and units”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-foundation-lead -->

**Answer.**

This course follows namespaces and formats through command completion, integrity, and management evidence. Use four sessions of roughly 25 minutes for the main path, with figure worksheets and questions for further study. Chapter 1 terminology and reference conventions are included.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §1.1-1.6; 4.1.3.9; 4.1.4.8; 4.1.5, printed pages 9-12,73-75,79-83, PDF pages 9-12,73-75,79-83

### Q02. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Reading map and units”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-foundation-rows -->

**Answer.**

- LBADS — data bytes = 2^LBADS — Add MS to obtain logical block size
- Format Index — Selects both LBAF and ELBAF — Data size alone is insufficient
- Specification family — Base defines common mechanisms — Dependencies carry separate Base citations

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §1.1-1.6; 4.1.3.9; 4.1.4.8; 4.1.5, printed pages 9-12,73-75,79-83, PDF pages 9-12,73-75,79-83

### Q03. How does “Reading map and units” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-foundation-example -->

**Answer.**

With LBADS=0Ch and MS=16, data occupies 4096 bytes and the complete logical block 4112 bytes. FID 28h configures limits while LID 28h reports the capability graph, despite their equal numbers.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §1.1-1.6; 4.1.3.9; 4.1.4.8; 4.1.5, printed pages 9-12,73-75,79-83, PDF pages 9-12,73-75,79-83

### Q04. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Reading map and units”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-foundation-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Worked values are teaching examples, not required device capabilities. Keep the different strengths of should, may, and shall.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §1.1-1.6; 4.1.3.9; 4.1.4.8; 4.1.5, printed pages 9-12,73-75,79-83, PDF pages 9-12,73-75,79-83

### Q05. What is the governing interpretation for “Namespace capacity and allocation”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-capacity-lead -->

**Answer.**

Separate logical address space from allocated resources before considering writes and deallocation. Returned data and allocation state answer different questions.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.1; 4.1.5.1, printed pages 13-14,85-93, PDF pages 13-14,85-93

### Q06. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Namespace capacity and allocation”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-capacity-rows -->

**Answer.**

- NSZE — Valid LBAs run from 0 to NSZE−1 — Out-of-range differs from capacity exhaustion
- THINP — Requires NUSE tracking when supported — Without support NUSE may remain NCAP
- Allocation — Write, the Copy destination, and WU allocate — Read/Verify do not change deallocation state

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.1; 4.1.5.1, printed pages 13-14,85-93, PDF pages 13-14,85-93

### Q07. How does “Namespace capacity and allocation” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-capacity-example -->

**Answer.**

NSZE=1000, NCAP=800, NUSE=600 can describe a valid thin namespace. LBA 900 is addressable, but additional allocation remains subject to the 800-block capacity.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.1; 4.1.5.1, printed pages 13-14,85-93, PDF pages 13-14,85-93

### Q08. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Namespace capacity and allocation”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-capacity-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

ANA state can zero reported NUSE/NVMCAP; those zeros alone do not establish data deletion.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.1; 4.1.5.1, printed pages 13-14,85-93, PDF pages 13-14,85-93

### Q09. What is the governing interpretation for “Ordering and Compare-and-Write”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-order-fused-lead -->

**Answer.**

First establish the ordering requirement, then decide whether conditional updating is needed. A fused operation protects comparison and update of the same LBA range, with atomic-size limits checked separately.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.2-2.1.3, printed pages 14-15, PDF pages 14-15

### Q10. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Ordering and Compare-and-Write”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-order-fused-rows -->

**Answer.**

- Ordinary I/O — Read/Write completion order for one LBA is not guaranteed — Use host completion dependencies
- Fused pair — Compare and Write use the same range — A mismatch should be rejected
- ACWU / NACWU — Bounds the fused atomic update — Atomic boundaries also apply

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.2-2.1.3, printed pages 14-15, PDF pages 14-15

### Q11. How does “Ordering and Compare-and-Write” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-order-fused-example -->

**Answer.**

For “replace A with B only if A is still present,” an independent Compare followed by Write permits an intervening write. A fused pair within its size and boundary limits provides the conditional atomic update.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.2-2.1.3, printed pages 14-15, PDF pages 14-15

### Q12. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Ordering and Compare-and-Write”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-order-fused-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Write failure does not retroactively change the Compare completion status; inspect both CQEs.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.2-2.1.3, printed pages 14-15, PDF pages 14-15

### Q13. What is the governing interpretation for “Normal, power-fail, and multiple atomicity”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-atomic-lead -->

**Answer.**

Read size, starting alignment, NSABP, and MAM together. Atomicity and persistence on nonvolatile media are separate checks; FUA/Flush do not establish ordering for other commands.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.4; 4.1.3.4; 5.9, printed pages 15-21,66-67,165, PDF pages 15-21,66-67,165

### Q14. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Normal, power-fail, and multiple atomicity”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-atomic-rows -->

**Answer.**

- AWUN / AWUPF — Sizes use zero-based encoding — AWUPF does not exceed AWUN
- NABO / NABSN / NABSPF — Boundaries occur at offset + k × size — Decode each field and its unreported cases
- MAM — Each atomic subrange has its own guarantee — Fused operations still use Single mode
- FID 0Ah.DN — DN=1 releases normal-atomicity requirements — Power-fail guarantees remain

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.4; 4.1.3.4; 5.9, printed pages 15-21,66-67,165, PDF pages 15-21,66-67,165

### Q15. How does “Normal, power-fail, and multiple atomicity” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-atomic-example -->

**Answer.**

For decoded boundary size 8 blocks and offset zero, a 12-block write starting at LBA 4 splits into [4..7] and [8..15]. Under MAM each part is atomic, not one transaction. Raw AWUN=7h represents eight blocks.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.4; 4.1.3.4; 5.9, printed pages 15-21,66-67,165, PDF pages 15-21,66-67,165

### Q16. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Normal, power-fail, and multiple atomicity”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-atomic-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Do not copy the §3.3.2.2 example equating NAWUN=8h with eight blocks: distinguish raw zero-based fields from decoded example sizes. Failed writes may still complete DMA, so buffer transfer completion is not media success.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.4; 4.1.3.4; 5.9, printed pages 15-21,66-67,165, PDF pages 15-21,66-67,165

### Q17. What is the governing interpretation for “Capabilities, opcodes, and status”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-support-status-lead -->

**Answer.**

Build a command/Feature/log capability matrix starting from controller type. A data pointer may reference user data or merely control descriptors.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.2; 3.1; 3.3, printed pages 22-27, PDF pages 22-27

### Q18. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Capabilities, opcodes, and status”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-support-status-rows -->

**Answer.**

- Read 02h / Write 01h — Mandatory I/O commands — Administrative controllers do not process I/O
- Get LBA Status 86h — Optional Admin command — Capability belongs to I/O controllers
- SC 80h — SCT distinguishes LBA Out of Range and other meanings — Record opcode, NSID, SCT, SC, and DNR
- FID / LID — 05h and 0Ah are mandatory NVM Features — Feature support differs from Persistent Event Log recording

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.2; 3.1; 3.3, printed pages 22-27, PDF pages 22-27

### Q19. How does “Capabilities, opcodes, and status” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-support-status-example -->

**Answer.**

Copy opcode 19h has low bits 01b because the host supplies source descriptors; it does not require the host to retransmit all user data being copied.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.2; 3.1; 3.3, printed pages 22-27, PDF pages 22-27

### Q20. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Capabilities, opcodes, and status”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-support-status-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

NSID FFFF FFFFh is not accepted by every command; Figure 22 permits it only for the specifically noted Flush/Cancel paths.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.2; 3.1; 3.3, printed pages 22-27, PDF pages 22-27

### Q21. What is the governing interpretation for “Read/Write data and completion”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-read-write-lead -->

**Answer.**

Check range, buffer, PI, and completion separately to distinguish addressing errors, format mismatches, and media failures.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.4; 3.3.6, printed pages 48-51,53-56, PDF pages 48-51,53-56

### Q22. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Read/Write data and completion”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-read-write-rows -->

**Answer.**

- CDW10 / CDW11 — Low/high 32 bits of SLBA — NLB=0 still requests one block
- CDW12 — LR, FUA, PRINFO, STC, CETYPE, NLB — The DTYPE area is reserved for Read
- CDW13 — CETYPE selects DSM or CEV interpretation — Write also carries DTYPE/DSPEC
- MPTR — Used for separate metadata — Do not split metadata between both mechanisms

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.4; 3.3.6, printed pages 48-51,53-56, PDF pages 48-51,53-56

### Q23. How does “Read/Write data and completion” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-read-write-example -->

**Answer.**

With SLBA=100, NLB=7, LBADS=12, and no metadata, Read covers 100..107 and 32768 bytes. An FUA Read commits the corresponding data before retrieving it from media; the host still orders dependent Writes.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.4; 3.3.6, printed pages 48-51,53-56, PDF pages 48-51,53-56

### Q24. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Read/Write data and completion”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-read-write-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

On CQE failure retain SCT/SC and the range; FUA or successful DMA does not replace the completion result. With nonzero CETYPE, low CDW13 bits cannot be decoded as DSM hints.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.4; 3.3.6, printed pages 48-51,53-56, PDF pages 48-51,53-56

### Q25. What is the governing interpretation for “Compare and Verify answer different questions”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-compare-verify-lead -->

**Answer.**

Expected-content comparison, integrity verification, and ordinary Read provide different evidence. Compare excludes PI from metadata comparison and checks PI separately as requested.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.1; 3.3.5, printed pages 27-30,51-53, PDF pages 27-30,51-53

### Q26. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Compare and Verify answer different questions”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-compare-verify-rows -->

**Answer.**

- Compare — A miscompare returns Compare Failure — PI can be checked on both host and media paths
- Verify — No data-buffer transfer — Verified data still counts toward Data Units Read
- VSL / NVMVFYS — The variant selects recommended size or a hard limit — Nonzero VSL uses 2^n × minimum page size

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.1; 3.3.5, printed pages 27-30,51-53, PDF pages 27-30,51-53

### Q27. How does “Compare and Verify answer different questions” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-compare-verify-example -->

**Answer.**

To determine whether stored contents equal zero, Compare can use a zero-filled expected buffer. Successful Verify establishes this integrity check, not that the contents equal zero.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.1; 3.3.5, printed pages 27-30,51-53, PDF pages 27-30,51-53

### Q28. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Compare and Verify answer different questions”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-compare-verify-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Verify with PRACT=1 returns Invalid Field in Command. Treating Verify as a zero-length Read or Compare as a data-return command leads to incorrect buffer setup.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.1; 3.3.5, printed pages 27-30,51-53, PDF pages 27-30,51-53

### Q29. What is the governing interpretation for “Copy: source descriptors, contiguous destination, partial failure”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-copy-lead -->

**Answer.**

Calculate the expanded destination range before checking formats, limits, overlap, and atomicity. Copy reduces host data movement but is not an unconditional transaction.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.2, printed pages 30-44, PDF pages 30-44

### Q30. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Copy: source descriptors, contiguous destination, partial failure”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-copy-rows -->

**Answer.**

- NR / NLB — Source count and per-range block count are zero-based — Check MSRC, MSSRL, and MCL
- FCO — Formats 2h/3h can request fast copy only — Inspect DNR after Fast Copy Not Possible
- Overlap — Formats 2h/3h prohibit source/destination overlap within one namespace — Formats 0h/1h need their separate overlap rules
- NVMCSA — Revision 1.3 treats the destination as one write command — MAM, size, and boundary limits still apply

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.2, printed pages 30-44, PDF pages 30-44

### Q31. How does “Copy: source descriptors, contiguous destination, partial failure” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-copy-example -->

**Answer.**

Two descriptors with NLB=3 and SDLBA=100 write 100..103 and 104..107: eight blocks total. DW0=1 does not prove that the second or any later range is entirely unmodified.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.2, printed pages 30-44, PDF pages 30-44

### Q32. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Copy: source descriptors, contiguous destination, partial failure”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-copy-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

FCO constrains the method, not the latency of every operation. Atomicity value FFFFh represents 65536 blocks; Copy can exceed that size, so it does not make all Copy commands atomic.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.2, printed pages 30-44, PDF pages 30-44

### Q33. What is the governing interpretation for “Copy PI compatibility and transformation”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-copy-pi-lead -->

**Answer.**

Classify whether source and destination use PI, then choose PRINFOR.PRACT and PRINFOW.PRACT. Every source must fit the selected mode.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.2.3-3.3.2.4; 5.3.2.5, printed pages 40-43,146-150, PDF pages 40-43,146-150

### Q34. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Copy PI compatibility and transformation”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-copy-pi-rows -->

**Answer.**

- PI → PI, 0/0 — Matching formats: pass-through — Checking remains controlled by check bits
- PI → PI, 1/1 — Matching formats: replace — Check the read path and generate write PI
- No PI → PI — Corresponding formats and write PRACT=1: insert — Destination metadata cannot include other content
- PI → No PI — Corresponding formats and read PRACT=1: strip — Source metadata must be PI-only

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.2.3-3.3.2.4; 5.3.2.5, printed pages 40-43,146-150, PDF pages 40-43,146-150

### Q35. How does “Copy PI compatibility and transformation” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-copy-pi-example -->

**Answer.**

A 4096+8-byte namespace with 16b PI can copy to 4096+0 bytes under the corresponding-format conditions. A 4096+16-byte source with eight extra metadata bytes cannot use that strip exception.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.2.3-3.3.2.4; 5.3.2.5, printed pages 40-43,146-150, PDF pages 40-43,146-150

### Q36. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Copy PI compatibility and transformation”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-copy-pi-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Sections 5.3.2.5.1/.2 interchange references to Figures 177–180. Cross-check their actual captions with §3.3.2.4.2: 0/0 passes PI through and 1/1 replaces it.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.2.3-3.3.2.4; 5.3.2.5, printed pages 40-43,146-150, PDF pages 40-43,146-150

### Q37. What is the governing interpretation for “Dataset Management and three processing limits”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-dsm-lead -->

**Answer.**

Determine whether each block satisfies all three limits before applying NVMDSMSV. Separate range/hint validity, attribute processing obligations, and actual media actions.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.3, printed pages 44-48, PDF pages 44-48

### Q38. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Dataset Management and three processing limits”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-dsm-rows -->

**Answer.**

- AD / IDW / IDR — Deallocate/integral-write/integral-read hints — Combinations are permitted
- Limits nonzero, variant=0 — Exceeding a limit returns Command Size Limit Exceeded — All fitting blocks require attribute processing
- Limits nonzero, variant=1 — Should process the portion satisfying the limits — Do not report Size Limit Exceeded for this reason
- All limits=0 — Variant=1: no limits reported; variant=0: unsupported — All three fields must be zero or all nonzero

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.3, printed pages 44-48, PDF pages 44-48

### Q39. How does “Dataset Management and three processing limits” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-dsm-example -->

**Answer.**

With DMRL=2, DMSL=1048, ranges of 1024 and 512 blocks, and a nonrestrictive DMRSL, variant=1 admits the first range and 24 blocks of the second. This does not guarantee deallocation of 1048 blocks.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.3, printed pages 44-48, PDF pages 44-48

### Q40. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Dataset Management and three processing limits”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-dsm-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Do not reuse the Write NLB encoder for DSM LLB. Zero-based encoding undercounts the range by one; LLB=0 does not mean one block.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.3, printed pages 44-48, PDF pages 44-48

### Q41. What is the governing interpretation for “Reading deallocated/unwritten blocks”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-dealloc-lead -->

**Answer.**

First determine whether successful reading is permitted, then interpret returned bytes. Allocation status, DRB, and PI have separate conditions.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.3.2.1; 4.1.3.3, printed pages 47-48,66, PDF pages 47-48,66

### Q42. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Reading deallocated/unwritten blocks”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-dealloc-rows -->

**Answer.**

- DAE / DULBE — DAE is capability; DULBE is enablement — DULBE defaults to zero
- DRB=000b — Does not mean arbitrary old data — Section 3.3.3.2.1 limits it to zeros or FFh
- PI after deallocation — Tag bytes return FFh; Guard is FFh or CRC — Use DLFEAT.GDS

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.3.2.1; 4.1.3.3, printed pages 47-48,66, PDF pages 47-48,66

### Q43. How does “Reading deallocated/unwritten blocks” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-dealloc-example -->

**Answer.**

One zero-filled Read does not prove successful sanitize; it may reflect DRB on deallocated blocks. Conversely, a DULBE error alone does not establish a media defect.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.3.2.1; 4.1.3.3, printed pages 47-48,66, PDF pages 47-48,66

### Q44. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Reading deallocated/unwritten blocks”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-dealloc-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Successful Read/Verify does not reallocate the block; writing changes that state.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.3.2.1; 4.1.3.3, printed pages 47-48,66, PDF pages 47-48,66

### Q45. What is the governing interpretation for “Write Uncorrectable, Write Zeroes, and whole-namespace zeroing”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-zero-uncorrectable-lead -->

**Answer.**

Neither command transfers a host user-data payload, but both change namespace semantics. Identify range mode before checking PI and size limits.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.7-3.3.8, printed pages 56-61, PDF pages 56-61

### Q46. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Write Uncorrectable, Write Zeroes, and whole-namespace zeroing”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-zero-uncorrectable-rows -->

**Answer.**

- Write Uncorrectable — Marks blocks so later reads can report Unrecovered Read Error — Interpret WUSL with NVMWUSV
- Write Zeroes PI — PRCHK=000b, STC=0 — PRACT=1 is recommended for valid PI
- WZSL / WZDSL — Select the applicable limit using DEAC — Neither limit applies with NSZ=1
- LBACZ — One on a successful NSZ command reports the entire namespace — Zero reports the specified range

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.7-3.3.8, printed pages 56-61, PDF pages 56-61

### Q47. How does “Write Uncorrectable, Write Zeroes, and whole-namespace zeroing” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-zero-uncorrectable-example -->

**Answer.**

Successful Completion with NSZ=1 but LBACZ=0 means only the range was zeroed. An older controller may ignore unsupported NSZ; command success alone does not establish whole-namespace zeroing.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.7-3.3.8, printed pages 56-61, PDF pages 56-61

### Q48. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Write Uncorrectable, Write Zeroes, and whole-namespace zeroing”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-zero-uncorrectable-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

DEAC=0 does not prohibit deallocation: the controller may still deallocate when zero-read conditions hold. A failed Write Zeroes can also have cleared some contents.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.3.7-3.3.8, printed pages 56-61, PDF pages 56-61

### Q49. What is the governing interpretation for “Format, Host Behavior, and extended LBAs”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-format-lead -->

**Answer.**

Formatting can change block counts and field applicability; re-identify before constructing buffers. Do not confuse capability lists with the active format.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.2; 4.1.3.7, printed pages 62-63,68-69, PDF pages 62-63,68-69

### Q50. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Format, Host Behavior, and extended LBAs”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-format-rows -->

**Answer.**

- PI / PIL — PI=0 disables protection; 1/2/3 select its type — This revision requires PIL=0, placing PI last
- MSET — One: extended LBA; zero: separate metadata — Ignored when MS=0
- LBAFEE — FID 16h byte 2, valid values zero/one — ELBAS also gates extended formats
- STS — Format cannot freely change STS to a new nonzero value — Namespace creation can establish a new configuration

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.2; 4.1.3.7, printed pages 62-63,68-69, PDF pages 62-63,68-69

### Q51. How does “Format, Host Behavior, and extended LBAs” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-format-example -->

**Answer.**

For 64b Guard with MS=16, first check ELBAS, LBAFEE=1, the corresponding LBAF/ELBAF, and PI capability. Setting Format PI=1 alone does not select 64b Guard.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.2; 4.1.3.7, printed pages 62-63,68-69, PDF pages 62-63,68-69

### Q52. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Format, Host Behavior, and extended LBAs”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-format-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

PI types 1/2/3 and Guard widths 16/32/64 are separate dimensions. NSZE/NCAP can change after formatting, and old LBA Range Type hints may need updating.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.2; 4.1.3.7, printed pages 62-63,68-69, PDF pages 62-63,68-69

### Q53. What is the governing interpretation for “Basic Feature scopes and exceptions”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-basic-features-lead -->

**Answer.**

Identify scope, units, and saveability when reading Features. Get, Set, and Supported Capabilities responses do not share one payload interpretation.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.3.1-4.1.3.4, printed pages 64-67, PDF pages 64-67

### Q54. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Basic Feature scopes and exceptions”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-basic-features-rows -->

**Answer.**

- FID 03h — 4096-byte contiguous buffer; up to 64 64-byte entries — NUM is zero-based; each new Set replaces prior information
- FID 05h.TLER — 100 ms units, timed from error-recovery start — Zero means no timeout; applies to LR-enabled commands
- FID 03h attributes — Hide/Overwriteable are host-use hints — They do not establish security isolation or data protection
- FID 02h extension — Idle-exit reference is an NPWG-sized Read — Other commands may exceed that latency limit

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.3.1-4.1.3.4, printed pages 64-67, PDF pages 64-67

### Q55. How does “Basic Feature scopes and exceptions” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-basic-features-example -->

**Answer.**

TLER=5 gives an error-recovery limit of 500 ms, not a 500 ms deadline measured from SQ submission. LBA Range Type NUM=0 represents one entry.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.3.1-4.1.3.4, printed pages 64-67, PDF pages 64-67

### Q56. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Basic Feature scopes and exceptions”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-basic-features-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Figure 92 persistence applies only to nonsaveable Features; saveable ones follow saved/default rules. A controller need not validate every LBA Range Type field, so successful Set does not establish that all ranges are sensible.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.3.1-4.1.3.4, printed pages 64-67, PDF pages 64-67

### Q57. What is the governing interpretation for “Identify: multiple structures for one namespace”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-identify-lead -->

**Answer.**

Write down the roles of CNS, CSI, NSID, and Format Index for each query. Zero-filled results have different meanings across queries and do not always mean absent or unsupported.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.5, printed pages 83-110, PDF pages 83-110

### Q58. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Identify: multiple structures for one namespace”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-identify-rows -->

**Answer.**

- CNS 00h / 05h — Basic/extended NVM namespace fields — FLBAS selects the active FIDX; MC/DPC are capabilities
- CNS 01h / 06h — Common-location AWUN fields and NVM-specific limits — 06h VSL/WZSL fields require variant bits
- CNS 11h / 1Bh — Allocated-namespace information — Different from active-namespace queries
- CNS 09h / 0Ah — Capability queries by FIDX — Common=No fields are zeroed
- CNS 16h — Namespace granularity list — GDM determines descriptor-to-format mapping

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.5, printed pages 83-110, PDF pages 83-110

### Q59. How does “Identify: multiple structures for one namespace” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-identify-example -->

**Answer.**

For NSID=7, read FLBAS and use that index in both LBAF and ELBAF. To query capabilities of FIDX=3 before creation, use 09h/0Ah, CSI=0, NSID=0, FIDX=3, plus common capabilities from CNS08h.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.5, printed pages 83-110, PDF pages 83-110

### Q60. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Identify: multiple structures for one namespace”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-identify-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

The “zoned namespace” wording in §4.1.5.10.1 conflicts with its NVM context. This course interprets it as the NVM namespace under CSI=00h and retains the source location for review.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.5, printed pages 83-110, PDF pages 83-110

### Q61. What is the governing interpretation for “LBAF, ELBAF, and unique-attribute formats”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-format-list-lead -->

**Answer.**

The basic entry gives data/metadata sizes and relative performance; the extended entry gives PI format and Storage Tag allocation. Query unique-attribute entries individually instead of assuming common capabilities.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.5.1; 4.1.5.3; 5.6, printed pages 85-94,96-102,160-162, PDF pages 85-94,96-102,160-162

### Q62. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “LBAF, ELBAF, and unique-attribute formats”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-format-list-rows -->

**Answer.**

- LBAF — LBADS, MS, RP — RP is a relative class for a specified workload
- ELBAF — PIF, QPIF, STS — QPIF applies only to qualified type
- FLBAS — FIDXU and FIDXL form the index — MTELBA is a separate metadata bit
- NULBAF — Appended after common formats — 09h/0Ah retrieve individual capabilities

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.5.1; 4.1.5.3; 5.6, printed pages 85-94,96-102,160-162, PDF pages 85-94,96-102,160-162

### Q63. How does “LBAF, ELBAF, and unique-attribute formats” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-format-list-example -->

**Answer.**

Raw NLBAF=3 and NULBAF=2 give four common formats and two unique-attribute formats: six total, indices 0..5. Figure 192 uses conceptual counts; do not substitute raw NLBAF without decoding it.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.5.1; 4.1.5.3; 5.6, printed pages 85-94,96-102,160-162, PDF pages 85-94,96-102,160-162

### Q64. What misinterpretation is most likely in “LBAF, ELBAF, and unique-attribute formats”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-format-list-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

LBADS=9 means 512 bytes and LBADS=12 means 4096 bytes. The §5.3.1.4.1 example equating LBADS=0 with 512 bytes is a source inconsistency and must not drive command construction.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.5.1; 4.1.5.3; 5.6, printed pages 85-94,96-102,160-162, PDF pages 85-94,96-102,160-162

### Q65. What is the governing interpretation for “Namespace creation: format, mask, granularity”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-namespace-create-lead -->

**Answer.**

Query Format Index capabilities before filling host-specified fields; do not use an entire unmodified Identify Namespace structure as the create payload.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.6; 4.1.5.8; 5.8, printed pages 108,110-113,165, PDF pages 108,110-113,165

### Q66. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Namespace creation: format, mask, granularity”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-namespace-create-rows -->

**Answer.**

- NSZE / NCAP — Values are specified in logical blocks — Convert before comparing with byte granularities
- LBSTM — Must satisfy PIC/PIFA masking constraints — Violations return Invalid Field in Command
- GDM / ND — GDM=0 uses descriptor zero for all formats — ND is zero-based
- Completion — Successful creation includes the requested formatting — Attachment is a separate management action

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.6; 4.1.5.8; 5.8, printed pages 108,110-113,165, PDF pages 108,110-113,165

### Q67. How does “Namespace creation: format, mask, granularity” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-namespace-create-example -->

**Answer.**

With NSG=NCG=1 MiB and logical block size 4096, NSZE=NCAP=256 makes the allocation fully addressable. Choosing 257 may leave extra unaddressable allocation under the hints, but that alone is not a rejection reason.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.6; 4.1.5.8; 5.8, printed pages 108,110-113,165, PDF pages 108,110-113,165

### Q68. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Namespace creation: format, mask, granularity”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-namespace-create-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Masking Not Supported requires all significant Storage Tag mask bits to be one, not zero. Placement fields do not acquire enabled-FDP semantics when FDP is unsupported or disabled.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.6; 4.1.5.8; 5.8, printed pages 108,110-113,165, PDF pages 108,110-113,165

### Q69. What is the governing interpretation for “FDP: placement, RUHs, and observable data”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-fdp-lead -->

**Answer.**

Creation establishes placement relationships; handle status describes operation, and statistics/events explain later media movement. These evidence types are not interchangeable.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.2.1; 4.1.4.6-4.1.4.7; 4.1.6.3, printed pages 26,79,110-113, PDF pages 26,79,110-113

### Q70. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “FDP: placement, RUHs, and observable data”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-fdp-rows -->

**Answer.**

- NPHNDLS — At most 128 and no more than the configuration RUH count — Zero invokes controller-selection and sharing rules
- EARUTR / RUAMW — Estimated remaining seconds / writable logical blocks — EARUTR=0 means unreported; not a lifetime guarantee
- LID 22h — HBMW/MBMW include the specified NVM write-class commands — Includes Copy destination, Zeroes, and Uncorrectable
- LID 23h event 0h — LBAV governs LBA validity — NLBAM=FFFFh means at least FFFFh

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.2.1; 4.1.4.6-4.1.4.7; 4.1.6.3, printed pages 26,79,110-113, PDF pages 26,79,110-113

### Q71. How does “FDP: placement, RUHs, and observable data” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-fdp-example -->

**Answer.**

If two namespaces share RUH 5 and one uses FIDX=2, creating the other with FIDX=3 violates the shared-RUH Format Index rule even if both have 4 KiB data blocks.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.2.1; 4.1.4.6-4.1.4.7; 4.1.6.3, printed pages 26,79,110-113, PDF pages 26,79,110-113

### Q72. What misinterpretation is most likely in “FDP: placement, RUHs, and observable data”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-fdp-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

The LBA in a Media Reallocated event is one member of the moved set, not a complete list; ignore it when LBAV=0.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §3.2.1; 4.1.4.6-4.1.4.7; 4.1.6.3, printed pages 26,79,110-113, PDF pages 26,79,110-113

### Q73. What is the governing interpretation for “NVM extensions to AER, SMART, and error records”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-log-events-lead -->

**Answer.**

Use events to direct investigation, then decode logs using their scope and command-set definitions. Classify commands correctly when interpreting statistics instead of guessing from opcode names.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §1.4.2; 4.1.1; 4.1.3.5; 4.1.4.1-4.1.4.4, printed pages 10-11,62,67,75-77, PDF pages 10-11,62,67,75-77

### Q74. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “NVM extensions to AER, SMART, and error records”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-log-events-rows -->

**Answer.**

- LBASIN / RLCCN — FID0Bh bits 13/22 — Enable LBA Status / Rate Limiting notices
- SMART units — Convert to 512-byte units, then apply Base counter encoding — One 4 KiB block is not one Data Unit
- Read categories — Data Units Read includes Verify; Host Read includes Copy — Compare and Read belong to both categories
- Persistent Event 06h — Create/single-delete records contain FLBAS and DPS — Both fields are reserved for delete-all

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §1.4.2; 4.1.1; 4.1.3.5; 4.1.4.1-4.1.4.4, printed pages 10-11,62,67,75-77, PDF pages 10-11,62,67,75-77

### Q75. How does “NVM extensions to AER, SMART, and error records” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-log-events-example -->

**Answer.**

A Self-test record with FLBA=100 and valid=1 identifies one failing LBA, not a clean bill of health for all others. Error Information’s “lowest LBA” semantics cannot be applied to FLBA.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §1.4.2; 4.1.1; 4.1.3.5; 4.1.4.1-4.1.4.4, printed pages 10-11,62,67,75-77, PDF pages 10-11,62,67,75-77

### Q76. What misinterpretation is most likely in “NVM extensions to AER, SMART, and error records”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-log-events-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

The Rate Limiting log uses CSI, while most other listed logs do not; do not mix command-set definitions for the same LID.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §1.4.2; 4.1.1; 4.1.3.5; 4.1.4.1-4.1.4.4, printed pages 10-11,62,67,75-77, PDF pages 10-11,62,67,75-77

### Q77. What is the governing interpretation for “LBA Status: notices, scans, and recovery”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-lba-status-lead -->

**Answer.**

Potentially unrecoverable does not mean every block necessarily fails to read. Identify ATYPE, check buffer capacity and completion condition, then arrange data recovery.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.3.6; 4.1.4.5; 4.2.1; 5.2.1, printed pages 67-68,77-79,114-122, PDF pages 67-68,77-79,114-122

### Q78. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “LBA Status: notices, scans, and recovery”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-lba-status-rows -->

**Answer.**

- MNDW / RL — MNDW is zero-based dwords; RL=0 runs through NSZE−1 — RL=0 does not query one block
- NLSD / CMPC — Actual descriptor count / completion reason — CMPC=1 means more data or incomplete scan; 2 means complete
- LSIPI / LSIRI — 100 ms units; host cannot change the poll interval — Set returns the closest supported value
- RAE / LSGC — Read chunks with RAE=1; RAE=0 clears the event and allows updates — Reread the header and check generation
- TLBAAG — 02h may report allocation at a larger granularity — A mixed unit is reported allocated as a whole

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.3.6; 4.1.4.5; 4.2.1; 5.2.1, printed pages 67-68,77-79,114-122, PDF pages 67-68,77-79,114-122

### Q79. How does “LBA Status: notices, scans, and recovery” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-lba-status-example -->

**Answer.**

NLSLNE=0 with nonzero ESTULB is not an all-clear: examine the full ranges of attached namespaces. Recover suspect LBAs from another reliable source and rewrite them; later queries remove successfully rewritten entries unless newly detected again.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.3.6; 4.1.4.5; 4.2.1; 5.2.1, printed pages 67-68,77-79,114-122, PDF pages 67-68,77-79,114-122

### Q80. What misinterpretation is most likely in “LBA Status: notices, scans, and recovery”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-lba-status-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Command success with CMPC=1 does not mean the whole range was scanned. Log RNLB and detailed-descriptor NLB are zero-based, while NLSD is an actual count.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.3.6; 4.1.4.5; 4.2.1; 5.2.1, printed pages 67-68,77-79,114-122, PDF pages 67-68,77-79,114-122

### Q81. What is the governing interpretation for “Performance Characteristics attributes”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-performance-feature-lead -->

**Answer.**

This Feature reports or manages performance attributes; its standard latency class is not a service guarantee for arbitrary workloads.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.3.8, printed pages 69-73, PDF pages 69-73

### Q82. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Performance Characteristics attributes”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-performance-feature-rows -->

**Answer.**

- R4KARL — Average-latency range for standardized 4 KiB random reads — 00h means unreported
- MSVSPA / USVSPA — Saveable capacity / unused capacity — Indices can be noncontiguous
- PAID / ATTRL — 128-bit identifier / valid vendor bytes — ATTRL is at most FE0h
- RVSPA — Delete the saved value to return to default — The data-buffer contents are unused

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.3.8, printed pages 69-73, PDF pages 69-73

### Q83. How does “Performance Characteristics attributes” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-performance-feature-example -->

**Answer.**

R4KARL=0Eh means 50 μs ≤ average latency <100 μs, not 14 μs. When reading the C0h list, match ATTRTYP with Get SEL and use PAID to interpret vendor payloads.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.3.8, printed pages 69-73, PDF pages 69-73

### Q84. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Performance Characteristics attributes”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-performance-feature-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Set with ATTRI=00h or C0h returns Invalid Field in Command. Vendor-byte meanings require a vendor definition and cannot be invented as standard fields.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.3.8, printed pages 69-73, PDF pages 69-73

### Q85. What is the governing interpretation for “Rate Limiting configuration fields”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-rate-config-lead -->

**Answer.**

Obtain supported targets from LID 28h, then check HLS/SLS and the soft-controller count. Record requested limits separately from attainable device capabilities.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.3.9; 4.1.5.4; 5.10, printed pages 73-75,106,165-168, PDF pages 73-75,106,165-168

### Q86. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Rate Limiting configuration fields”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-rate-config-rows -->

**Answer.**

- TGT / TID — CDW11[23:16] / [15:0] — TGT=0 is the standard controller target
- RLC — RLE bit15; RLM=0 Hard, 1 Soft — Soft support requires Hard support
- BWSF — 0/1/2 = 1/10/100 MiB/s; 3/4/5 = 1/10/100 GiB/s — Multiply the value by the scale
- WRIOPSR / WRBWR — Write numerator divided by read denominator — Every ratio component byte must be nonzero

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.3.9; 4.1.5.4; 5.10, printed pages 73-75,106,165-168, PDF pages 73-75,106,165-168

### Q87. How does “Rate Limiting configuration fields” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-rate-config-example -->

**Answer.**

BWSF=1 and TBWV=50 specify 500 MiB/s. WBWV/WIOPS govern writes, while total consumption is weighted by WRBWR/WRIOPSR; total limits are not simply read limits.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.3.9; 4.1.5.4; 5.10, printed pages 73-75,106,165-168, PDF pages 73-75,106,165-168

### Q88. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Rate Limiting configuration fields”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-rate-config-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Limits for an unconfigured target are vendor-specific, not necessarily unlimited. The opening §5.10 references interchange Hard/Soft sections: 5.10.1 is Hard and 5.10.2 is Soft.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.3.9; 4.1.5.4; 5.10, printed pages 73-75,106,165-168, PDF pages 73-75,106,165-168

### Q89. What is the governing interpretation for “The Rate Limiting log is a capability graph”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-rate-graph-lead -->

**Answer.**

Validate structure bounds before analyzing bandwidth bottlenecks. Port capability differs from shared Endurance Group capability; do not simply add all reported numbers.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.4.8; 5.10.3, printed pages 79-83,168-172, PDF pages 79-83,168-172

### Q90. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “The Rate Limiting log is a capability graph”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-rate-graph-rows -->

**Answer.**

- LPL / offsets — Lengths and pointers use dword units — Byte offset = dword offset ×4
- NP / NC / NST — All are zero-based counts — NNSMAD is an actual count
- SC / SI — Subsystem/domain/EG/namespace and its ID — Interpret scope and avoid double-counting shared nodes
- RLMA — Maximum read/write bandwidth/IOPS — Relevant size/queue-depth workload conditions apply

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.4.8; 5.10.3, printed pages 79-83,168-172, PDF pages 79-83,168-172

### Q91. How does “The Rate Limiting log is a capability graph” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-rate-graph-example -->

**Answer.**

Two PCIe ports may share one Endurance Group. If controller 0 consumes all EG bandwidth, the extra port does not create more media bandwidth for controller 1. Both controllers may reference one descriptor for identical EG access capabilities.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.4.8; 5.10.3, printed pages 79-83,168-172, PDF pages 79-83,168-172

### Q92. What misinterpretation is most likely in “The Rate Limiting log is a capability graph”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-rate-graph-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Examples in Figures 196/198 contain inconsistent offsets, byte ranges, and LPL. This course redraws the relationships and checks offset×4, descriptor length, and LPL bounds instead of treating the examples as executable binary fixtures.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.4.8; 5.10.3, printed pages 79-83,168-172, PDF pages 79-83,168-172

### Q93. What is the governing interpretation for “Hard/Soft modes and token-bucket examples”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-rate-modes-lead -->

**Answer.**

Interpret results using capability, configured limits, and actual demand. A configured ratio does not force a fixed throughput ratio at every instant; internal resources and workload still matter.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.10.1-5.10.2; Appendix A, printed pages 166-168,176-177, PDF pages 166-168,176-177

### Q94. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Hard/Soft modes and token-bucket examples”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-rate-modes-rows -->

**Answer.**

- Hard — Proportional sharing under demand and resource shortage — A configured ceiling is not a performance floor
- Soft — May consume unused capacity — Multiple soft targets share it in proportion to limits
- Write tokens — Total bytes × WRBWR; write bytes; total IOPS × WRIOPSR; one write IOPS — Check each of four buckets
- Read tokens — Total bytes and one total IOPS — Does not consume write-only buckets

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.10.1-5.10.2; Appendix A, printed pages 166-168,176-177, PDF pages 166-168,176-177

### Q95. How does “Hard/Soft modes and token-bucket examples” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-rate-modes-example -->

**Answer.**

Teaching setup: a 4 KiB Write with WRBWR=2 and WRIOPSR=3 consumes 8 KiB total-bandwidth, 4 KiB write-bandwidth, three total-IOPS, and one write-IOPS token. A 4 KiB Read consumes only 4 KiB total-bandwidth and one total-IOPS token.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.10.1-5.10.2; Appendix A, printed pages 166-168,176-177, PDF pages 166-168,176-177

### Q96. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Hard/Soft modes and token-bucket examples”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-rate-modes-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Insufficient tokens defer commands rather than drop them. Partial processing is allowed, but completion cannot precede processing of the entire command.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.10.1-5.10.2; Appendix A, printed pages 166-168,176-177, PDF pages 166-168,176-177

### Q97. What is the governing interpretation for “Alignment, granularity, and performance hints”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-alignment-lead -->

**Answer.**

Decode raw fields into blocks, then evaluate starting alignment and length granularity. Meeting only one can still cause read-modify-write.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.2.2, printed pages 122-129, PDF pages 122-129

### Q98. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Alignment, granularity, and performance hints”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-alignment-rows -->

**Answer.**

- NPWG / NPWA — Meet both length and start recommendations — First check NSFEAT.OPTPERF
- NPRG / NPRA / NORS — Guide read optimization — First check OPTRPERF
- NPDG / NPDGL — Alternative deallocate-granularity fields — Select via OPTPERF; Large fields do not universally add one
- NOIOB / NABO — Optimal I/O boundary differs from atomic offset — I/O can be split to satisfy multiple conditions

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.2.2, printed pages 122-129, PDF pages 122-129

### Q99. How does “Alignment, granularity, and performance hints” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-alignment-example -->

**Answer.**

With decoded NPWG=8 and NPWA=8, writing LBAs 8..15 meets both. Writing 9..16 also has eight blocks but crosses two units and may require reading old data at both ends.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.2.2, printed pages 122-129, PDF pages 122-129

### Q100. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Alignment, granularity, and performance hints”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-alignment-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

The source’s read-modify-write diagrams illustrate a possible mechanism, not a mandatory internal implementation on every SSD. Reformatting can invalidate old alignment hints.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.2.2, printed pages 122-129, PDF pages 122-129

### Q101. What is the governing interpretation for “Metadata transfer and PI placement”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-metadata-lead -->

**Answer.**

Metadata need not consist entirely of PI. Mark data, non-PI metadata, and PI separately before computing host-buffer size and CRC coverage.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.6; 5.2.3; 5.3, printed pages 22,129-131, PDF pages 22,129-131

### Q102. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Metadata transfer and PI placement”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-metadata-rows -->

**Answer.**

- Extended LBA — DPTR addresses interleaved data+metadata — MSET/MTELBA reflect the selection
- Separate buffer — DPTR addresses data; MPTR addresses metadata — PRP metadata is physically contiguous; SGL metadata may be scattered
- PI location — Valid current formats put PI at the metadata end — CRC covers preceding non-PI metadata

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.6; 5.2.3; 5.3, printed pages 22,129-131, PDF pages 22,129-131

### Q103. How does “Metadata transfer and PI placement” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-metadata-example -->

**Answer.**

For eight blocks, data=4096, MS=16, PRACT=0: the extended buffer is 32896 bytes; separate buffers are 32768 data bytes and 128 metadata bytes.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.6; 5.2.3; 5.3, printed pages 22,129-131, PDF pages 22,129-131

### Q104. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Metadata transfer and PI placement”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-metadata-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

PI placement at the end and separate-versus-extended metadata are independent choices; DIF/DIX terminology does not replace namespace-format settings.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.6; 5.2.3; 5.3, printed pages 22,129-131, PDF pages 22,129-131

### Q105. What is the governing interpretation for “16/32/64b Guard and qualified PI”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-pi-formats-lead -->

**Answer.**

Select the format with PIF; only PIF=11b delegates Guard width to QPIF, subject to QPIFS and STMLA. DPS separately selects protection type.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.3.1; 4.1.5.3, printed pages 97-102,130-138, PDF pages 97-102,130-138

### Q106. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “16/32/64b Guard and qualified PI”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-pi-formats-rows -->

**Answer.**

- 16b Guard — 2-byte Guard + 2-byte App + 4-byte space — STS=0..32
- 32b Guard — 4-byte Guard + 2-byte App + 10-byte space — STS=16..64
- 64b Guard — 8-byte Guard + 2-byte App + 6-byte space — STS=0..48
- STMLA — Bit masking / byte masking / no masking — Qualified type and QPIFS determine applicability

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.3.1; 4.1.5.3, printed pages 97-102,130-138, PDF pages 97-102,130-138

### Q107. How does “16/32/64b Guard and qualified PI” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-pi-formats-example -->

**Answer.**

With 64b Guard and STS=18, the high 18 bits of the 48-bit space form Storage Tag and the low 30 bits form Reference Tag. Total PI remains 16 bytes; increasing STS does not enlarge it.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.3.1; 4.1.5.3, printed pages 97-102,130-138, PDF pages 97-102,130-138

### Q108. What misinterpretation is most likely in “16/32/64b Guard and qualified PI”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-pi-formats-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

This revision defines qualified type, so PIF=11b is not universally reserved. Reference Tag is absent when STS consumes the entire space; Storage Tag is absent when STS=0.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.3.1; 4.1.5.3, printed pages 97-102,130-138, PDF pages 97-102,130-138

### Q109. What is the governing interpretation for “CRC parameters, bit order, and known vectors”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-crc-lead -->

**Answer.**

Check polynomial, initialization, reflection, final XOR, and storage order together. Validate known vectors before integrating a PI parser.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.3.1.1-5.3.1.3, printed pages 131-137, PDF pages 131-137

### Q110. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “CRC parameters, bit order, and known vectors”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-crc-rows -->

**Answer.**

- CRC-16 — Guard CRC defined by SBC-4 — NVM does not support the optional DIX IP checksum
- CRC-32C — Polynomial 1EDC6F41h — 4 KiB zero vector → 98F94189h
- CRC-64/NVME — Reflected-register example 123456789 → AE8B14860A799888h — 4 KiB zero vector → 6482D367EB22B64Eh
- Coverage — Data plus metadata preceding PI — Exclude PI itself

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.3.1.1-5.3.1.3, printed pages 131-137, PDF pages 131-137

### Q111. How does “CRC parameters, bit order, and known vectors” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-crc-example -->

**Answer.**

The CRC-64 result for 4 KiB of FFh is C0DDBA7302ECA3ACh. If the zero vector passes but the incrementing-byte vector fails, inspect byte/bit order rather than changing the polynomial to fit.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.3.1.1-5.3.1.3, printed pages 131-137, PDF pages 131-137

### Q112. What misinterpretation is most likely in “CRC parameters, bit order, and known vectors”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-crc-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Figure 161 lists Check=11199E506128D175h; a conventional LSB-first register computes AE8B14860A799888h for 123456789. They are 64-bit reversals. All four Figure 163 4 KiB vectors directly match that register result. State this representation discrepancy rather than changing the polynomial to fit one Check value. CRC is not cryptographic authentication.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.3.1.1-5.3.1.3, printed pages 131-137, PDF pages 131-137

### Q113. What is the governing interpretation for “Packing Storage/Reference Tags into Dwords”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-tag-layout-lead -->

**Answer.**

Determine total space width, split the tags, then pack command Dwords. Similar names do not make Write values interchangeable with Read expected values.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.3.1.4, printed pages 137-141, PDF pages 137-141

### Q114. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Packing Storage/Reference Tags into Dwords”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-tag-layout-rows -->

**Answer.**

- 16b Guard, STS=0 — CDW14 contains the 32-bit reference — CDW2/3 are ignored for this tag
- 32b Guard, STS=32 — CDW2 low16 + CDW3 high16 carry Storage — CDW3 low16 + CDW14 carry the 48-bit Reference
- 64b Guard, STS=18 — CDW3 low16 + CDW14 high2 carry Storage — CDW14 low30 carry Reference

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.3.1.4, printed pages 137-141, PDF pages 137-141

### Q115. How does “Packing Storage/Reference Tags into Dwords” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-tag-layout-example -->

**Answer.**

For 64b Guard, STS=18, Storage Tag=0x12345, Reference Tag=0x2A: CDW3 low16=0x48D1 and CDW14=(1<<30)|0x2A=0x4000002A. Read uses expected tags in the same layout.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.3.1.4, printed pages 137-141, PDF pages 137-141

### Q116. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Packing Storage/Reference Tags into Dwords”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-tag-layout-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Figure 171 gives a CDW3 Storage Tag range overlapping the next row. Figures 166 and 170 support interpreting it as high16; this is an explicitly identified engineering interpretation of a source inconsistency.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.3.1.4, printed pages 137-141, PDF pages 137-141

### Q117. What is the governing interpretation for “Combining PRACT with PRCHK/STC”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-pi-checking-lead -->

**Answer.**

First determine whether namespace PI is enabled, then choose a processing branch by command direction and metadata size. Evaluate checking bits and special disable values afterward.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.5; 5.3.2-5.3.3, printed pages 21-22,141-152, PDF pages 21-22,141-152

### Q118. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Combining PRACT with PRCHK/STC”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-pi-checking-rows -->

**Answer.**

- Write, PRACT=1 — Insert PI when MS=PI; replace it when MS>PI — This generation branch ignores PRCHK/STC
- Read, PRACT=1 — Perform requested checks; strip only when MS=PI — MS>PI still returns metadata including PI
- Type 1 / Type 2 — Reference increments per block — Type1 initial value must match relevant low SLBA bits
- Type 3 — Should not compare a computed reference — An RTCHK rejection uses Invalid Protection Information
- Disable sentinels — Type 1/2 disable all PI checks when Application Tag=FFFFh; Type 3 additionally requires an all-ones Reference Tag, if defined — Overrides PRCHK/STC settings
- Masks — A zero mask bit excludes comparison — Storage masking also obeys STMLA

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.5; 5.3.2-5.3.3, printed pages 21-22,141-152, PDF pages 21-22,141-152

### Q119. How does “Combining PRACT with PRCHK/STC” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-pi-checking-example -->

**Answer.**

For 16b Guard, MS=16, Read PRACT=1, the host still receives 16 metadata bytes. With MS=8 it receives data only. The same PRACT value produces different buffer lengths under different MS.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.5; 5.3.2-5.3.3, printed pages 21-22,141-152, PDF pages 21-22,141-152

### Q120. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Combining PRACT with PRCHK/STC”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-pi-checking-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

STC here means Storage Tag Check, not Self-test Code. Both Compare input paths can perform PI checking, while PI bytes are excluded from ordinary metadata comparison.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §2.1.5; 5.3.2-5.3.3, printed pages 21-22,141-152, PDF pages 21-22,141-152

### Q121. What is the governing interpretation for “NVM behavior under ANA and Reservations”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-ana-reservations-lead -->

**Answer.**

Check namespace access state separately from access permissions; path state does not establish reservation ownership.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.1; 5.11, printed pages 119,172-173, PDF pages 119,172-173

### Q122. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “NVM behavior under ANA and Reservations”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-ana-reservations-rows -->

**Answer.**

- ANA Identify — NUSE/NVMCAP return zero in Inaccessible/Persistent Loss — This does not mean media was erased
- ANA FID05h — Get is restricted in Inaccessible/Persistent Loss/Change — Use the corresponding ANA status
- Write Exclusive / Exclusive Access — For nonholders, the former allows read-like commands; the latter conflicts with read-like and write-like commands — Nonholder write-like commands conflict for both
- Registrants Only / All Registrants — Write Exclusive variants allow reads by anyone and writes by registrants; Exclusive Access variants allow reads/writes only by registrants — Copy checks each source as read and its destination as write
- Reservations — Check the matrix for read-like/write-like commands — Holder, registrant, and type all matter

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.1; 5.11, printed pages 119,172-173, PDF pages 119,172-173

### Q123. How does “NVM behavior under ANA and Reservations” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-ana-reservations-example -->

**Answer.**

Two PCIe controllers of one SSD may share a namespace. Controller 1 can have an accessible path yet be unable to Write due to reservation type and its registration state; Read permissions require a separate matrix lookup.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.1; 5.11, printed pages 119,172-173, PDF pages 119,172-173

### Q124. What misinterpretation is most likely in “NVM behavior under ANA and Reservations”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-ana-reservations-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

A reservation does not universally block all nonholder I/O; types such as Write Exclusive and Exclusive Access have different read rules.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.1; 5.11, printed pages 119,172-173, PDF pages 119,172-173

### Q125. What is the governing interpretation for “LBA Migration Queue and change tracking”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-migration-queue-lead -->

**Answer.**

The queue records changed ranges and sequence markers rather than complete new data. The host still retrieves data with appropriate I/O and handles the logging-stop boundary caused by a full queue.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.8; 5.7, printed pages 113-114,162-164, PDF pages 113-114,162-164

### Q126. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “LBA Migration Queue and change tracking”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-migration-queue-rows -->

**Answer.**

- LBACIR — 00: range; 01: whole namespace; 10: no range — Determine field validity first
- ESA — 001 start/resume; 010 stop; 011 suspend; 111 full — Full means logging stopped
- DLBA / CDQP — Deallocation flag / entry phase — DLBA=0 may still describe a deallocation-related change
- RALBAS — ATYPE02h covers changes during the start command when supported — Start/stop markers need not precede Track Send CQE

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.8; 5.7, printed pages 113-114,162-164, PDF pages 113-114,162-164

### Q127. How does “LBA Migration Queue and change tracking” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-migration-queue-example -->

**Answer.**

Three sequential Writes may become one range entry, so entry count is not write-command count. After ESA=111b, the host cannot assume subsequent changes continue to be logged.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.8; 5.7, printed pages 113-114,162-164, PDF pages 113-114,162-164

### Q128. What misinterpretation is most likely in “LBA Migration Queue and change tracking”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-migration-queue-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

This lesson covers NVM LBA change tracking without expanding into other transport protocols or resource-export formats. Address queue capacity and consistency before restarting tracking.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.8; 5.7, printed pages 113-114,162-164, PDF pages 113-114,162-164

### Q129. What is the governing interpretation for “NVM rules for Sanitize and Media Verification”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-sanitize-lead -->

**Answer.**

Identify target, operation state, and allocation before deciding what can be verified. The initiating CQE and completion of the sanitize operation require different evidence.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.7; 5.12, printed pages 113,173-175, PDF pages 113,173-175

### Q130. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “NVM rules for Sanitize and Media Verification”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-sanitize-rows -->

**Answer.**

- LID81h — Tracks operation status/progress — Successful initiation is not operation completion
- Error Information — The NVM LBA field returns zero during sanitize — This NVM extension still obeys the Base command allowlist
- Media Verification Read — PRCHK=000b, STC=0 — Requesting checking gives Invalid Field in Command
- Allocated media — Return actual data if readable; error if unreadable — Qualifying reads return Successful Media Verification Read

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.7; 5.12, printed pages 113,173-175, PDF pages 113,173-175

### Q131. How does “NVM rules for Sanitize and Media Verification” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-sanitize-example -->

**Answer.**

In Media Verification, a Read without PI checking can ignore integrity errors when allocated media remains readable and return the specific success status. Repeated reads of one LBA may differ, so ordinary stable-value assumptions do not apply.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.7; 5.12, printed pages 113,173-175, PDF pages 113,173-175

### Q132. What misinterpretation is most likely in “NVM rules for Sanitize and Media Verification”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-sanitize-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Zero-filled reads after sanitize are not sufficient proof of success, and not every method is expected to return zeros. Namespace and subsystem sanitize scopes are not interchangeable.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §4.1.7; 5.12, printed pages 113,173-175, PDF pages 113,173-175

### Q133. What is the governing interpretation for “NVM alignment constraints for Key Per I/O”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-key-per-io-lead -->

**Answer.**

Determine applicability from KPIOCAP and namespace status before decoding the CETYPE/CEV command extension. This NVM supplement does not fully define key creation or management.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.5; 4.1.5, printed pages 91-92,105,160, PDF pages 91-92,105,160

### Q134. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “NVM alignment constraints for Key Per I/O”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-key-per-io-rows -->

**Answer.**

- KPIOCAP — Support and subsystem/namespace scope — Do not rely on an enable bit alone
- KPIOSNS / KPIOENS — Namespace support / enablement — Enable must be zero without support
- KPIODAAG — Zero-based logical-block granularity — Both start and length must conform

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.5; 4.1.5, printed pages 91-92,105,160, PDF pages 91-92,105,160

### Q135. How does “NVM alignment constraints for Key Per I/O” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-key-per-io-example -->

**Answer.**

Raw KPIODAAG=7 represents eight-block granularity. SLBA=16 and length=8 fit; SLBA=17 or length=7 do not, even when all other PI fields are correct.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.5; 4.1.5, printed pages 91-92,105,160, PDF pages 91-92,105,160

### Q136. What misinterpretation is most likely in “NVM alignment constraints for Key Per I/O”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-key-per-io-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Invalid Key Tag and alignment-related Invalid Field in Command require different investigations; key-tag rejection is not necessarily a PI checksum error.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.5; 4.1.5, printed pages 91-92,105,160, PDF pages 91-92,105,160

### Q137. What is the governing interpretation for “NVM units and priorities for Streams”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-streams-lead -->

**Answer.**

Use two size levels: Stream Write Size and the larger stream granularity. They may be integer multiples of namespace hints, but this is not guaranteed for every namespace.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.2.2.3; 5.13, printed pages 128-129,175, PDF pages 128-129,175

### Q138. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “NVM units and priorities for Streams”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-streams-rows -->

**Answer.**

- SWS — Recommended write size in blocks — Should be a multiple of NPWG
- SGS × SWS — Length of the stream granularity — Guides stream deallocate alignment/length
- Priority — Prefer Streams attributes when Streams are used — Otherwise use namespace hints

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.2.2.3; 5.13, printed pages 128-129,175, PDF pages 128-129,175

### Q139. How does “NVM units and priorities for Streams” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-streams-example -->

**Answer.**

Decoded SWS=8 blocks and SGS=4 give a 32-block stream granularity. An eight-block Write can meet SWS, while deallocating one full granularity unit uses 32 blocks.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.2.2.3; 5.13, printed pages 128-129,175, PDF pages 128-129,175

### Q140. What misinterpretation is most likely in “NVM units and priorities for Streams”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-streams-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Streams hints, FDP placement, and namespace atomicity are different concepts; equal sizes do not prove they identify the same internal media unit.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.2.2.3; 5.13, printed pages 128-129,175, PDF pages 128-129,175

### Q141. What is the governing interpretation for “Memory-based resource export template”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-export-template-lead -->

**Answer.**

The template compatibility interface and underlying device capabilities are separate layers. Check namespace-format compatibility, then configure limits no greater than underlying capabilities; do not advertise capabilities the template does not permit.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.4.1-5.4.1.1, printed pages 152-159, PDF pages 152-159

### Q142. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Memory-based resource export template”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-export-template-rows -->

**Answer.**

- Identity and version — CAP.CSS=1, VS=020300h; NVM VER=010200h — The template fixes Base 2.3/NVM 1.2; the enclosing PDF revision does not upgrade it
- Controller limits — MDTS, RAB, NCQS, NSQS, MQES, AWUN/AWUPF are bounded by underlying support — NCQS/NSQS are zero-based
- Namespace compatibility — LBAF0 must match underlying LBADS/MS, with MS=0; DPS/KPIOENS/CWP must be zero — The controller handles Format Index remapping
- Observable defaults — Error entries and SMART are zero; firmware active slot is 1 — Support lists, Feature defaults, and Identify exceptions have fixed rules

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.4.1-5.4.1.1, printed pages 152-159, PDF pages 152-159

### Q143. How does “Memory-based resource export template” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-export-template-example -->

**Answer.**

Underlying NCQS=7 supports eight queues; configured NCQS=3 permits four queues, not three. A zero namespace NGUID requires a valid NUUID.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.4.1-5.4.1.1, printed pages 152-159, PDF pages 152-159

### Q144. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Memory-based resource export template”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-export-template-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

Figure 190 says Controller in its caption, but its payload is namespace configuration: decode ENSID, LBAF0, NGUID, and NUUID. Figure 189 teaches the permitted local fields only; other identity fields are not expanded.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.4.1-5.4.1.1, printed pages 152-159, PDF pages 152-159

### Q145. What is the governing interpretation for “Exported-state length and consistency”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-export-state-lead -->

**Answer.**

Read the fixed 64-byte header, then validate variable length and suspension evidence. Configuration state and runtime state differ in purpose and setting constraints; do not share their payload parsers.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.4.1.2, printed pages 159-160, PDF pages 159-160

### Q146. Which concepts or conditions must be distinguished in “Exported-state length and consistency”?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-export-state-rows -->

**Answer.**

- Feature values — Saves arbitration, power, temperature, error recovery, queues, interrupt, atomicity, and AEC — These are current values, not Figure 187 defaults
- CSATTR.CP — 1 means suspended throughout processing — 0 does not mean there was no suspension at all
- NVMECSS — Total length = 64 + 4 × NVMECSS bytes — NVMECS is absent when zero

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.4.1.2, printed pages 159-160, PDF pages 159-160

### Q147. How does “Exported-state length and consistency” apply to a concrete calculation or operational scenario?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-export-state-example -->

**Answer.**

With NVMECSS=16, NVMECS occupies 64 bytes and the complete structure 128 bytes. Check multiplication, addition, and receive-buffer bounds before decoding nested VER.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.4.1.2, printed pages 159-160, PDF pages 159-160

### Q148. What misinterpretation is most likely in “Exported-state length and consistency”, and how is it debugged?

<!-- qa:nvm-command-set-1.3-nvmcs-export-state-pitfall -->

**Answer.**

This describes memory-based controller state. A single Feature value cannot establish successful subsystem migration without complete state and suspension evidence.

> Source: NVME-NVM-CS-1.3, Rev. 1.3, §5.4.1.2, printed pages 159-160, PDF pages 159-160
